client: I've been feeling completely overwhelmed at work lately. My boss just dumped two huge new projects on me with impossible deadlines, and I'm already struggling to keep up with my current workload. I'm not sure talking about it will help because the deadlines aren't going to change, and I can't just say no to my boss.
therapist: I hear how overwhelmed you're feeling with these new demands piling up on top of your existing workload. It sounds like you're caught between feeling unable to meet these expectations but also powerless to push back. What thoughts come up for you when you imagine discussing this workload with your boss?

client: I just keep thinking my boss will see me as weak or incompetent if I say I can't handle the workload. My stomach knots up imagining that conversation because last time I mentioned being overwhelmed, they just said "everyone's busy right now" and walked away. It feels like no matter what I do, I'll either fail at my work or fail at standing up for myself.
therapist: I can sense how painful this dilemma feels - like you're stuck between impossible choices where either path feels like failure. That past experience where your concerns were dismissed understandably makes this situation feel even more hopeless. What would it look like if we explored some small ways you might approach this differently while still honoring your very real concerns about how you're perceived?

client: I appreciate you acknowledging how stuck I feel, but honestly I'm not sure small changes will make a difference. Every time I try to approach things differently, I just end up feeling like I'm pretending to be someone I'm not. And then the guilt comes back because I worry people can tell I'm faking it.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of guilt and self-doubt whenever you try to make changes, like you're betraying your authentic self. That must feel exhausting to constantly question whether your actions come across as genuine. What does being "your authentic self" look like to you in this work situation?

client: Being my authentic self at work feels like a constant balancing act. I want to be professional and competent, but I also worry that I come across as too rigid or detached, like I’m not letting people see the real me. At the same time, when I try to be more open or casual, I feel like I’m faking it, like I’m putting on a performance just to fit in. It’s exhausting to second-guess every interaction. I don’t even know what “authentic” looks like anymore—it feels like I’m always betraying some part of myself.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful extremes - feeling too rigid when you're professional, and inauthentic when you're casual - with no version of yourself that feels truly right. That constant self-monitoring must be incredibly draining. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to not have to perform or "get it right" in every interaction?

client: That sounds nice in theory, but I don't know how to just stop performing. If I'm not careful about how I act, I worry people will think I'm weird or incompetent. The idea of letting go makes me feel exposed and vulnerable, like I'd be opening myself up to judgment.
therapist: I hear how scary that vulnerability feels - like removing that careful performance might leave you unprotected from judgment. That fear makes complete sense when you've felt dismissed in the past. What would happen if we explored small, low-stakes ways you might experiment with being slightly more authentic, perhaps with people who feel safer?

client: I get what you're saying about trying small steps, but even that feels terrifying. Like last week, I almost told my coworker I was feeling overwhelmed but then panicked and just made a joke instead. The idea of being vulnerable with anyone, even "safe" people, makes my chest feel tight. What if they don't actually care or think I'm being dramatic?
therapist: That tightness in your chest shows how deeply vulnerable this feels - like even small risks of opening up could lead to being dismissed or judged. Your reaction makes perfect sense when past attempts to share your struggles were minimized. What would it feel like to acknowledge that panic response without judging yourself for having it?

client: It does feel like a tightness, like I'm bracing myself for rejection before I even say anything. But when you say not to judge myself for it, that's hard - because part of me thinks I *should* be able to handle this better by now. The panic just makes me feel weak.
therapist: I hear that double pain - both the physical tension of anticipating rejection, and then the added layer of judging yourself for having that very human reaction. It's understandable to feel frustrated when your body reacts in ways that don't match how you wish you could respond. What might it feel like to treat that panicked part of yourself with the same compassion you'd show a close friend in this situation?

client: I get what you're saying about compassion, but it's hard to imagine actually doing that. When my friend is anxious I can be kind, but with myself it just feels like I'm making excuses for being weak. The physical tension makes everything worse because it's like my body is betraying me before anything even happens.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real disconnect between the kindness you can extend to others and what you allow for yourself - almost like you're holding yourself to impossible standards while giving others grace. That physical tension isn't betrayal, it's your body trying to protect you from anticipated pain. What might shift if we viewed that protective response not as weakness, but as your system's way of trying to keep you safe?

client: I get what you're saying about my body trying to protect me, but it doesn't feel protective when I'm lying awake at night with my heart racing. It just feels like I'm failing at being calm. And about the standards thing... I know I'm hard on myself, but if I don't push myself, who will? People rely on me to be strong.
therapist: I hear how exhausting it is to feel like you're constantly battling your own body and emotions while carrying the weight of others' expectations. That pressure to always be strong while feeling anything but calm must be incredibly draining. What would it feel like to imagine, just for a moment, that being truly strong could include moments of acknowledging how hard this is for you?

client: I guess I never really thought about strength that way. To me, being strong has always meant pushing through no matter what, even when I’m falling apart inside. The idea of acknowledging how hard it is feels... almost like admitting defeat. But honestly, I’m so tired of pretending everything’s fine all the time. It’s just hard to let go of that mindset, you know? I worry that if I stop pushing myself to be strong, I’ll just collapse under all this pressure.
therapist: It sounds like that "push through at all costs" mindset has been both your armor and your cage - keeping you going while also trapping you in exhaustion. Letting go of that familiar pattern does feel scary, like you might fall apart completely. What would it be like to explore small ways to honor your limits without seeing it as defeat?
